ledger.note: 1218: Uglich becomes the seat of a small princedom. Page: 'From 1218 until 1328, Uglich was the seat of a small princedom.' The Konstantin of Rostov page's infobox lists Vladimir Konstantinovich of Uglich among Konstantin's sons; Konstantin died on 2 February 1218. The region is the town and a 30 km disc.

1328: the Uglich princes sell their rights to Moscow. Page: 'From 1218 until 1328, Uglich was the seat of a small princedom. At that time, the local princes sold their rights to the great prince of Moscow.' The page dates the end of the princedom, not the sale. Afterwards the town is held by princes of Moscow's house (Konstantin Dmitriyevich, 'prince of Uglich and Pskov', Dmitry Donskoy page, whose '14 May 1389 - 1433' are his birth and death, not years of rule [reviewer g-eu-c 2026-11-01]), so the dossier keeps one state and records the change of line as a rename.

ledger.note: 1389: the Uglich and Bezhetsk lands stand outside the merged thrones. Donskoy page: 'Konstantin Dmitriyevich (14 May 1389 - 1433), prince of Uglich and Pskov', without saying how he came to hold Uglich. The page does not date any transfer of land; the year and region repeat the Vladimir-Suzdal dossier's loss (ledger 10, confidence 1), and the Uglich land was then a Moscow-dynasty appanage.

region.text: 29 cells in the Vladimir-Suzdal shape, read by the Vladimir-Suzdal dossier as the Bezhetsk country

ledger.note: 1415 (Cliopatria's year): the Bezhetsk country passes to Moscow. Page: 'In the early 15th century, the area of Bezhetsky Verkh was annexed by' the Grand Duchy of Moscow; 'Since 1433, Bezhetsk had its own prince, who was subordinate to the Grand Prince of Moscow.' The page gives no year for the annexation; this repeats the Moscow dossier's gain of 29 cells (ledger 20).

1462: Ivan III gives Uglich to his brother Andrey Bolshoy. Page: 'Grand Duke Ivan III of Moscow gave the town in 1462 to his younger brother Andrey Bolshoy (Andrey the Great).' The Ivan III page has the grant in Vasily II's will (undated): Andrey received 'Uglich, Bezhetsk, Verkh and Zvenigorod'.

1482 (Cliopatria's year): the Uglich country enters Moscow's shape, as the Moscow dossier records (ledger 35). The Ivan III page is silent on 1482 and dates the end of the appanage later: 'In 1491, Andrey Bolshoy was arrested by Ivan for refusing to aid the Crimean Khanate against the Golden Horde.' 'He died in prison in 1493, and Ivan seized his land.'

1482 (Cliopatria's year): the Uglich land ends as a separate holding of the map. The Ivan III page gives 1491 (arrest) and 1493 ('Ivan seized his land') for the end of Andrey Bolshoy's appanage; the dossier follows the Moscow dossier's 1482 so that the two agree, and the difference is flagged in the notes.

certainty.note: No page gives a frontier of the princedom or the appanage; it is the town and a radius, then the Vladimir-Suzdal dossier's cells.

notes: No Cliopatria row and no article of its own ('Principality of Uglich' is not a page; the Uglich article is the town's). Two phases on the pages: an independent princedom 1218-1328 (Uglich page), and from the sale of the princes' rights to Moscow (1328) an appanage of Moscow's house (Konstantin Dmitriyevich, prince of Uglich, born 1389, died 1433, years of rule not on the page; Andrey Bolshoy from 1462), with Bezhetsk under its own prince from 1433 'subordinate to the Grand Prince of Moscow'. The citing dossiers (Vladimir-Suzdal 1389; Moscow 1415 and 1482, all confidence 1) treat the Uglich-Bezhetsk lands as a separate holding between 1389 and 1482 because Cliopatria's Vladimir-Suzdal shapes keep drawing them outside Moscow's shape; the pages do not. The Vladimir-Suzdal dossier left the decision, state or part of Moscow, to this dossier: it is kept as a state from 1218 to 1482 so that the three dossiers agree, the 1328 sale and the Moscow-house princes are carried by a rename, and a gap-filler should decide whether 1328-1462 is simply Moscow's domain (the page reading) and Moscow's 1415/1482 gains and the Vladimir-Suzdal loss should name Moscow or nobody. End year: the Ivan III page dates Andrey Bolshoy's fall to 1491-1493 ('Ivan seized his land'); 1482 is Cliopatria's year as the Moscow dossier records it. The ruler strip is omitted: pages give only Konstantin Dmitriyevich (lived 1389-1433, years of rule not given) and Andrey Bolshoy (from 1462). The first prince Vladimir Konstantinovich has no date on any page opened (Uglich page silent). Ivan I's purchase of Uglich (cited by the Vladimir-Suzdal dossier from the Moscow page) was not found on the Donskoy page. No wars: no page opened dates any attack on Uglich (the Uglich page says only that Tatars burned the town, undated). Gazetteer: place 'Uglich' resolves.
